messages.subject: Warning Messages in Program Distance
parts:
Hey all,

I'm new to the email list so sorry if this seems like a basic question.

I ran some transects of birds that I am having some problems analyzing in D=
istance without getting warning messages. The most common are:

**Warning: Parameter 2 is at a lower bound. **
**Warning: Parameter 1 is at a lower bound. **
**Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **
**Warning: Size bias adjustment has increased expected cluster size. **

I am running the analysis as clusters of objects (birds). I have tried alt=
ering the key function and expansion but regardless of which I choose, I al=
ways get an error like the ones above. Can anyone on this List let me know=
what I might be doing wrong or how I can fix these warnings? Thanks in ad=
vance!

Liz Rogers
MA Student
Environmental Studies
UNC-Wilmington=

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Warning Messages in Program Distance
parts:
Elizabeth:

Don't panic. You aren't necessarily doing anything 'wrong' in your analyses.
But these warnings (at least the first 3) are suggesting to you that your data
are not necessarily well-behaved, and the software is having difficulty fitting
the usual sort of detection functions to your data.

The first 2 warnings are stating that the most appropriate estimate for the
parameter(s) of your detection functions are at the edge of their expected
values. Likewise the third warning is suggesting that there is a 'bump' in
birds detected at some distance away from the transect line. Distance wants to
try to fit that bump by making the detection function rise, but one principle of
distance sampling is that detectability falls as a function of perpendicular
distance. This dissonance is expressed by Distance with that third warning
message.

Don't simply accept whatever Distance produces for parameter estimates and
resulting detection functions. Take a hard look at your histograms; that will
illuminate the pathologies that are being described by these warnings.

The last warning states that rather than size bias correction resulting in an
adjusted expected cluster size smaller than the average detected cluster size,
the adjusted expected cluster size is larger than the average observed. That
is not inherently incorrect, rather it is unusual; so Distance has alerted you
to this. It is then your responsibility to scrutinise the size bias adjustment
calculations closely.

messages.author: 5900eadecec2d82d
messages.subject: Re: Warning Messages in Program Distance
parts:
Hi Liz,

The monotonicity and size bias warnings have been discussed in previous
postings to the list. As the list guidelines say, you should search the
archives before posting questions. To do this, go to
http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling.html
and type some key words into the Search Archives box (e.g.,
"monotonicity" or "size bias"). However, to save you time, I repeat one
of the answers about each topic below (there are others I did not copy).

The lower bounds issue has also been mentioned, but not very explicitly,
so I've written more on this at the end of this message.

Hope this is useful. Cheers, - Len

--------------------------------------
Monotonicity
--------------------------------------
Here's a repeat of what I wrote to the list on 11th December 2003:

--
Hi Scott,

I'm cc'ing my reply to the distance-sampling list as this is a question that
comes up fairly often:

On Wed, 10 Dec 2003 09:33:50 -0600, Scott Somershoe wrote:


> > Len, Thanks again for your help. I think things are rolling smoothly
> > now. One question, I get a warning saying "Parameters are being
> > constrained to obtain monotonicity." Is this a problem I need to
> > worry about?

The short answer is usually not.

Here's the long answer. Under most circumstances we expect a priori
that true detection function is a monotonicly non-increasing function of
distance from the point or line (i.e., the further the object is from
the point or line, the lower the probabilty of detection). Therefore, by
default, Distance tries to ensure that the fitted function is monotonic
non-increasing. It does this by evaluating the detection function g(x)
at a set of evenly spaced distances (x's)
from 0 (x0) to the truncation distance (x9), and it makes sure that
g(x0)>=g(x1)>=g(x2)>=... >= g(x9). There are other options in Model
Definition | Detection function | Constraints, and these are documented
in the online manual.

Under most circumstances, the fitted function does not come up against
this constraint -- in other words the data indicate that the function
should be monotonic non-increasing. However, under some circumstances
the data call for a non-monotonic function, so the constraint is
triggered and that is why you get the warning message. The estimates you
end up with are no longer maximum likelihood estimates, but are
constrained maximum likelihood estimates.

The commonest case where this happens is where you have a relatively
small dataset and just by chance there is a small "bump" at some
distance, which Distance would try to fit with an extra adjustment term,
were it not for the monotonicity constraint. Such models are usually
over-parameterized (too many adjustment terms) and are not chosen using
model selection criteria such as AIC. You can see this in the D4Ducknest
example project -- the half-normal+cosine model gives a monotonicity
warning when the first cosine term is added, but then
that model has an AIC of 1.5 worse than the plain half-normal model, so
is not selected. See the Model Fitting page of results for that
analysis. (If you want to see the effect of the constraint, try running
an analysis with half- normal + 1 cosine adjustment manually selected
and no constraints.)

You can also get this occuring where there is a problem in your dataset
such as evasive movement of animals, which leads to "too few" animals
close to the line or point, and "too many" away from it. In this case,
you don't want to fit the data, but instead you want your fitted
detection function to be "too high" close to the line or point and "too
low" away from it. Fitting a hazard rate or half-normal key function
with few or no adjustments and monotonicity constraint turned on will
achieve this. (An alternative with such data is to put the data
into intervals, as I think has been discussed in previous postings.)

If a function that has been constrained is the one selected by Distance
then there is a minor problem with the estimate of the variance of f(0).
This is because the fit is no longer the maximum likelihood fit (because
of the constraint) so the theory used in deriving the variance isn't
valid. However, in practice this isn't something to worry about. In any
case, we recommend deriving final variance estimates for D or N using a
nonparametric bootstrap, resampling by transects, so the analytic
variance of f(0) becomes irrelevant.

So, in summary, if you see this message, you should look at the Model
Fitting page of results to see which function it was fitting when the
message occured. Was that function selected? If not, it's likely just a
symptom that the model not selected had too many parameters. Also look
again at your data and ask yourself why was the constraint hit -- is
there some problem in your data (such as evasive movement), or was it
likely due to one histogram bar being slightly higher than previous bars
just due to chance (as with the Ducknest data). The histogram plots and
Chi-sq goodness of fit tests will be useful in answering
this.

[...]

--------------------------------------
Size bias
--------------------------------------

Regarding size bias, I wrote the following as part of a message on 2nd
Feb 2004. There's also lots about size bias and methods of dealing with
a relationship between cluster size and detection probability in the
Introduction to Distance Sampling book (I don't have it to hand, so
can't root out the actual pages).

--
[...]

Regarding the size bias warning; we normally expect large clusters of
animals to be easier to detect than small clusters at large distances,
so a regression of cluster size against distance from the line has a
positive slope. For reasons outlined in the book (look in the index
under "size biased sampling"), the default regression in Distance is
actually log(cluster size) against detection probability, which we
expect to have a negative slope.

In some cases, the estimated slope can go the other way - i.e., the
regression of log(cluster size) against detection probability has a
positive slope. One obvious reason for this is that the slope is an
estimate, subject to sampling error, so it could just be chance.
Another is that the true slope really is positive: that you really are
more likely to record smaller clusters at greater distances from the
line (and so lower probability of detection). This can occur if you
underestimate cluster size at these larger distances (can't see the
whole cluster). The regression still works fine though -- the estimated
intercept at zero distance is still an unbiased estimate of average
cluster size in the population.

--------------------------------------
Parameters at a lower bound
--------------------------------------

I didn't find much explicit guidance on this one in the archives, so
here's an explanation. I'll assume you know what the parameters of each
detection function model are, and what order they come in - if not,
there's information about this in Chapter 8 of the online manual under
Output from CDS Analyses | About CDS Detection function formulae, and
subsequent pages (and also check the Intro to DS book, where the various
functions are explained in detail). All parameters in the key functions
get given constraints automatically by Distance. For example, the scale
parameter of the half-normal detection function can't be less than 0 --
but actually a value of 0 will cause problems so the default lower bound
is a small value (details of how this is calculated don't really matter
here). Similarly, the upper bound of the half normal in theory is
infinity, but in practice a large number is used to help the fitting
(after some large value, all bigger values have pretty much the same
likelihood, so it's best to do some constraining). You can actually
find out what the default constraints are by fitting a model with the
key function you're interested in and manually setting the number of
adjustment terms to zero (in the model definition, under Detection
function | Adjustment terms, choose manual selection and put 0 for Num
adj. params). Then, when you run the analysis, you'll see something
like this in the Results page Detection Fct/Global/Model fitting (the
following output comes from the ducknest example project):

Effort : 1600.000
# samples : 1
Width : 8.000000
Left : 0.0000000
# observations: 534

Model
Half-normal key, k(y) = Exp(-y**2/(2*A(1)**2))
A( 1) bounds = (0.80000E-01 , 0.10000E+07 )

You see the bounds above: 0.08 and 1000000.

I think it would be unusual for one to run into the default bounds, and
hence I'm a bit puzzled with your message that the parameter 1 (that is
A1) is at a lower bound. You should have a look and see what model it
occurred for, and so which parameter it corresponds to and see if you
can work out why it might have happened. Perhaps it was just something
that happened during fitting (you can see each iteration of the fitting
algorithm by choosing "Report results for each iteration of the
detection function fitting routine" in the Misc tab of the Model
Definition) and the final estimate is not at the boundary. Perhaps it
was for a model that was over-parameterized in any case (see previous
text about the monotonicity warning), and not a selected model.

The parameter 2 warning is more common, as this corresponds to the shape
parameter of a hazard rate key function, so my guess is that you got
this warning with the hazard rate function. In this case, the shape
parameter is constrained to have a lower bound of 1, for a minor
technical reason - here's what I get from the Ducknest sample project
when I manually select 0 adjustments:

Effort : 1600.000
# samples : 1
Width : 8.000000
Left : 0.0000000
# observations: 534

Model
Hazard Rate key, k(y) = 1 - Exp(-(y/A(1))**-A(2))
A( 1) bounds = (0.80000E-01 , 0.10000E+07 )
A( 2) bounds = ( 1.0000 , 20.000 )

Values slightly less than 1 are OK, but do indicate perhaps a sharp
spike in the data close to zero distance -- i.e., too many small
distances and not a nice shoulder to the detection function (see Intro
to DS book under shape criterion for why you want a nice wide shoulder).
If the data look OK, but you get this warning, you could try setting a
slightly smaller lower bound - to do this, go to the Model Definition |
Detection function | Constraints, and under "Bounds on key function
parameters" type in the number of key parameters (2 in the case of a
hazard rate with no stratification) and for the above scenario under
lower bound for Key 2 you'd enter a value less than 1 such as 0.5, and
then try re-running the model. Check the resulting fit is sensible.

Hope this is useful to you. Please contact me off the list if this
doesn't make sense, or doesn't help you work out what's happening with
your dataset. If I've been really unclear, or there's something I've
missed in my explanation, then we could post a follow-up message to the
list for the benefit of others who may have the same problem in future.

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Warning Messages in Program Distance
parts:
> > The last warning states that rather than size bias correction resulting in an
> > adjusted expected cluster size smaller than the average detected cluster size,
> > the adjusted expected cluster size is larger than the average observed. That
> > is not inherently incorrect, rather it is unusual; so Distance has alerted you
> > to this. It is then your responsibility to scrutinise the size bias adjustment
> > calculations closely.

Just to add to Eric's last comment, there are two relatively common
circumstances where this warning arises:

1. There is little or no effect of cluster size on detectability, and
just by chance, the estimated (usually small) correction happens to go
the 'wrong' way as a result of sampling variation.

2. Cluster size tends to be underestimated for more distant detections.
If size is accurately recorded for clusters on the line, but
underestimated for clusters away for the line, the correction will go
the 'wrong' way, and the warning will be issued, but in fact the method
is adjusting for underestimation of cluster size, so the adjusted
expected cluster size is larger than the average observed. In practice,
the method corrects for both size bias (which means large distant
clusters are more likely to be detected than small clusters at the same
distance) and underestimation of the size of more distant clusters, when
both biases are present.

Steve Buckland
